#6711. A Close Look At the 10 Key Autumn/Winter 2026 Bag Trends

Compared with the wave of house debuts for spring/summer, the fall/winter 2026 season was business as usual—sort of. Only a handful of inaugural showcases this time around, but the sophomore collections brought plenty of ideas to the fore, including an abundance of ready-to-wear and bag trends.

Pieter Mulier focused on the former in his last show for Alaïa after a five-year stint, which Vogue’s Sarah Mower described as “quiet perfectionism”. “It’s just really clothes for real people, not for an image,” Mulier said. “To reduce, reduce. No bags, no jewelry. Only beauty and clothes and a naked shoe. Because that’s what Azzedine was.”

Yet, during his tenure, Mulier delivered a number of It-bags, the most recent being his Le Teckel—meaning “sausage dog” in French, for its slimline shape—which will hold its value far beyond his departure. In fact, he could be credited with influencing the current streamlined, top-handle bag trend —the east-west—designed with the same tuck-under-your-arm spirit as the Le Teckel—which was present across recent runway shows.

Top handles in various iterations, including this popular east-west shape, acted as props for the 15 models cast at Prada, each of whom wore four layered looks that transformed as they walked the runway. Elsewhere, the intentionally undone Amazona 18 bag, introduced at Loewe by Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez, returned in a swathe of new colorways and finishes.

Chanel also went bold with bags this season, exhibiting everything from supersized shoulder bags and siren-red croc-embossed companions to delicately embroidered flap bags. The mood Anthony Vaccarello conveyed at Saint Laurent, however, was quite the opposite: skinny envelopes clasped by models on his carpeted runway. These clutch wallets accompanied Vaccarello’s step-and-repeat of suits that comprised the opening eight looks–a nod to the 60th anniversary of the Le Smoking, one of the house’s most revolutionary contributions to the industry.

Along with clutches, minaudières were also a prominent trend this season; these jewel-like purses—akin to special occasion jewelry—had a strong presence at Loewe, Dior, and Chanel. The newcomer this season was the U-Shape bag (also known as the half moon bag), seen at Stella McCartney, Louis Vuitton, Polo Ralph Lauren, and Tod’s; think of it as the new slouch bag. This season, croc-embossing also appeared across an array of accessories, especially in bags. For all upcoming holiday festivities, tassel bags feel like an elegant touch to add to any ensemble. While textured bags complement any cozy outfit.

Here, Vogue brings you seven standout trends from the collections that are worth shopping right now.

The east-to-west silhouette from season’s past is more prominent than ever. From Chanel’s punchy color to Bottega Veneta's more neutral options, the elongated silhouette shows up in top handles, shoulders, and tote bags. Then there is Fendi’s iconic baguette bag, the gift that keeps on giving. Sleek yet spacious, it packs a punch without overdoing it.

This season—from Saint Laurent shoulder bags to Prada’s pouch bags—animal print bags are taking charge in every silhouette. Leopard, cheetah, zebra, and fawn spots are key this fall and winter. An animal print bag can add that personality to any outfit; think of it as a neutral.

Crocodile, whether real exotic leather or embossed, made its mark this season, too, elevating the simplest of shapes with a tactile, high-gloss finish. Prada, Celine, Chanel, and Tory Burch all made a case for croco. Lean into the trend by adding a neutral or bold color to your wardrobe; this texture adds that ultimate touch of luxury.

Tassels were once used to adorn a home, bringing a bit of elegance and opulence. This season, with the resurgence of Art Deco glamour, designers have been inspired to incorporate them into modern-day dressing, as seen at Bottega Veneta, Lanvin, and Ulla Johnson. Lean into the trend with a tassel bag that makes for event dressing.

Top-handle bags bring an entirely different vibe to the act of carrying a bag, since they can only be grasped with one hand or slipped into the crook of an arm. No bother: you’ll want the profiles of the new bags from Hermès, Dior and Prada on full display. More rigid top-handles leaned into doctor bag territory with curved proportions (see Miu Miu, Balenciaga, Proenza Schouler), while others, such as Jonathan Anderson’s playful Cigale, offered a new everyday silhouette, fitting for night and day. This is the perfect bag to take from the office to an evening out, the ultimate investment for any wardrobe.

Winter is around the corner, and it's the perfect time to start building your cold-weather wardrobe. Pair a plush shearling bag (either lined or full-on plush); these bags are meant to complement your winter-cozy-yet-chic look. Available in an array of silhouettes, from pouch bags to tote bags, they are meant to complement any look, as seen at Simone Rocha, Bottega Veneta, and Fendi.

Shoulder bags are traditionally quite small, holding just a few belongings, but the shows offered a fresh crop of styles scaled up ever so slightly. They still fit snugly on the shoulder, tucking easily under the arm, with more room for everyday items–some (from the likes of Chanel, Miu Miu and Bottega Veneta) could even hold a laptop.

Consider the crescent bag the slouchy bag’s more sculptural cousin—still slouchy but not expressly relaxed. This season, the curved half moon (or U shape) silhouette was spotted everywhere from Dior to Tod’s, Polo, Stella, and Louis Vuitton. Choose from bigger sizes for day, or a smaller one for the evening. Think of this as the new slouch bag of the season.

Evening affairs—be they a wedding or a gala—call for accents that are a conversation starter. Designers interpreted the assignment differently, but many brought whimsy to it: Chanel strung a glossy pomegranate from a wristlet chain, while Dior turned the frog prince into a valiant dinner companion. From metal-finished to leather minaudieres, these bags are exquisite, almost like a jewelry piece that holds just the essentials.

Once upon a time, clutches were restricted to evening use, but recent seasons have changed that mindset. Look to the supple, pillowy pouches at Loewe, Bottega Veneta, and Stella McCartney, which would be just as fitting out on the town as they would on your morning commute. The clutch has proven to be a fashion favorite, especially this season; we have seen it worn during fashion week.

#6710. Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates

Squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta. Butternut is the easiest squash to source—not to mention easily found peeled and chopped (a blessing for those with more timid knife skills). But other winter squash like acorn or red kuri can stand in as desired. Whichever squash you select, a sharp, heavy chef’s knife is best for breaking down the chunky veg. But to make your life easier, microwave the squash for 1 to 2 minutes. It will slightly soften, making it simpler—and safer—to slice through.

Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.

More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.

Cook 1 medium butternut squash (1½–2 lb.), peeled, halved, seeds removed, cut into 1" pieces (about 6 cups), in a large pot of boiling salted water until very tender, 12–14 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer squash to a medium bowl. Reduce heat to low, cover pot, and leave on burner to keep warm.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium Dutch oven over medium-high. Add 1 lb. hot or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and break up into small pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, about 3 minutes. Continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until browned all over and just cooked through, 3–4 minutes more. Transfer to a plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to medium-low. Cook 3½ oz. Medjool dates (about 6), pitted, sliced lengthwise ¾" thick, in same pan, turning halfway though, until deeply browned, 3–4 minutes. Transfer to plate with sausage; season with salt.

Add remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil to pan. Add 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and reserved squash. Cook, scraping up browned bits and smashing squash with spoon to break up, until lightly browned and broken up into a chunky paste (pieces do not need to be even), about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, return cooking liquid in reserved pot to a boil over high heat. Cook 12 oz. short tube pasta (such as rigatoni) until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions (it will finish cooking in sauce). Drain, reserving 3 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid to squash and break up squash with spoon until a saucy consistency. Add pasta, another 1 cup pasta cooking liquid, and reserved sausage and dates. Increase heat to medium-high; cook, adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is al dente and coated in sauce, 2–3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. sherry vinegar or balsamic vinegar. Taste pasta and add more vinegar, salt and/or pepper if needed.

#6708. The Official Guide To Last-Minute Friendsgiving Appetizers, Based On How Much Time You Have

Consider us your official party-planning committee.

The holiday season is one of the busiest times of the year, so it’s no surprise that Friendsgiving can sneak up on you. If you put your name down to bring an appetizer and put off the planning until crunch time, don’t worry, last-minute appetizers are kind of our thing. Whether you’ve got days to plan ahead or minutes to whip together a party-worthy app, we’ve got you covered with these 10 Friendsgiving appetizers to bring to the party, based on how much time you have. Plus, these apps are so impressive, nobody will ever realize you almost showed up empty-handed.

Looking for more Friendsgiving recipes? Check out the rest of our last-minute Friendsgiving recipes and our top-rated Friendsgiving recipes.

You Want To Get A Jump Start The Night Before: Turkey Cheese Ball

This cheese ball is not only the most eye-catching appetizer you can add to your holiday menu, but it’s surprisingly easy to create. You’ll just have let it chill for about 3 hours in the refrigerator.

You Woke Up Early & Have Plenty Of Time: Sweet Potato Rolls

These rolls use sweet potatoes to make them even softer and fluffier, similar to our classic potato rolls. The tops are brushed with a honey butter and sprinkled with salt to play up both the savory and sweet side of a sweet potato.

You Still Have A Couple Hours To Spare: Cranberry Walnut Cheese Log

Salty, crunchy, and sometimes sweet, this pre-dinner treat is easy and infinitely adaptable for any season and occasion. Here, dried sweetened cranberries, walnuts, and fresh thyme conjure a holiday feeling, while a little honey complements the sweet-tart fruit.

You’re Still In Your Comfy Clothes: Green Bean Casserole Bites

Baked in crescent roll cups with crispy fried onions, a rich, creamy mushroom sauce, and tender-yet-snappy green beans, these handheld wonders hit every note. Have them as an appetizer or even on your plate as a biscuit substitute!

You’re Feeling Good With An Hour To Go: Sausage Stuffing Bites With Cranberry Sauce

Baked stuffing, inside the turkey or out, is a Thanksgiving staple for many families, although the particulars of the go-to recipe can vary. The only thing better than any of these stuffing recipes? MORE. STUFFING. Enter a bite-sized, stuffing-centered appetizer with a tangy, three-ingredient dipping sauce.

You’re Starting To Keep An Eye On The Clock: Brie & Green Bean Bundles

Perfect for a Thanksgiving potluck, these bundles of joy turn the classic green bean casserole into a handheld delight, all wrapped in flaky crescent dough. Wherever you choose to serve them, we guarantee one thing—these flaky and cheesy apps will go fast.

You Just Got A Last-Minute Text From The Host, Asking For Another App: Pumpkin Spice Hot Honey Brie Bites

Sweet and savory with a kick of heat, these pumpkin, Brie, and hot honey bites are the perfect fall appetizer. The honey provides the perfect balance for the sweetness of the pumpkin and the savory, melty Brie. Add a bit of fresh thyme and some roasted pecans, and you’ve got yourself a certified crowd-pleaser.

You’ve Got 30 Minutes To Make Some Magic Happen: Turkuterie

This Friendsgiving, keep your kitchen free of filching fingers by creating the most adorable charcuterie—err, turkuterie—board your friends and family will have ever seen. We’ve packed this cheese board with fruits and cheeses appropriate for an autumnal snack that everyone will want to gobble up!

You’ve Got One Shoe On Already: Cranberry Whipped Feta Dip

A holiday cheeseboard is great and all, but why go to all the trouble when you can make this sweet, salty, creamy, and tart dip with a fraction of the time and effort Fresh feta cheese is combined with herbs, garlic, and cream cheese, whipped until super-smooth, then topped with tart homemade cranberry sauce, toasted pistachios, and honey.

Oh No, Weren’t You Supposed To Bring Something?!: Antipasto Bites

When we need a last-minute appetizer for any party, we always turn to these antipasto skewers. They're ready in just 15 minutes, are perfectly shareable, and have all of the varied flavors and textures of an antipasto spread.

#6707. The Real-Life Wardrobe of Jamie Campbell Bower, Who Only Wears Suits If They’re McQueen

“I don’t know, I suppose I’m an artist,” Jamie Campbell Bower says with a laugh, after I ask him to describe himself. He’s correct, in more ways than one. If you’ve been consuming pop culture for the last decade and change, it’s less a matter of if you’ve seen the 37-year-old Londoner before, but where. He’s acted in some of the biggest franchises in Hollywood—including Twilight, Harry Potter, The Mortal Instruments, and Stranger Things—while also nurturing a multifaceted music career. As of this month, he’ll be heading to Middle-earth as Celeborn in the third season of Amazon Prime’s epic Lord of the Rings series, The Rings of Power.

During a hectic week of Rings of Power in New York City, Bower and I spent a quiet early morning talking about the bands that helped him find his style as a teenager, the difference between performing as an actor and a musician, and why he loves playing the bad guy.

All clothing and accessories, subject’s own. Coat by MM6 Maison Margiela. Sweater by John Lawrence Sullivan. Vintage skirt. Shoes by John Lawrence Sullivan. Sunglasses by Persol (throughout). Jewelry by Pianegonda.

Jamie Campbell Bower: It’s complexity. With any character, there has to be a level of complexity. Playing in the shadow self is really illuminating, to be Jungian. You have to know it in order for it to not take over. I found it particularly interesting to rationale and reason, even though this character was doing terrible things. I have always found it really interesting to dig away and find the why. So much of that character was really about isolation and pain and not feeling like they had a sense of belonging in the space for them. Obviously, they find this power that gives them this sense of safety. It becomes the wall, and it gives them purpose, and it hides them from the world and from being hurt. What draws me to any character is complexity and understanding the balance. It’s almost anthropological in a way.

It was amazing. I was so terrified on day one. I’m always nervous about joining any show, doing any gig. But I remember day one of actually shooting with other cast members, turning around to Nick Müller, our A-camera operator, and I just went, “Look, Nick, you’ve been here way longer than I have. If I’m in your way, just tell me to fucking move.”

I’d been a part of Twilight as well—joined that on the second movie after watching a cultural moment explode—and I was in that position again with Stranger Things. It was so big. I was joining this new world, but everyone was wicked and super kind. I made some amazing friends. I love Millie [Bobby Brown]. She’s just the best. She’s like my little sister, and also like my big sister at times as well. She’s got so much sage advice and is so brilliant at what she does and so driven. I am in awe of her, and I was from the moment I met her.

I’ve got the hand of Vecna. I took it out on Fallon [the other] night. I told this story, but I got my bag searched in Mexico City on the way in over the weekend. We pulled up and one of the people there looked at me—her eyes got big. She said, “Vecna.” I’ve got three massive fuck-off suitcases. They’re going through them and I’m like, “Look, I’ve got the hand of Vecna in here. Do you want to see it?” And then it ended up being the quickest bag search ever. I got some elf ears with me as well, both made by the same guy, Barrie Gower.

It was the summer when I was 15. I spent it wearing a visor with spiky hair, because I used to skate growing up in super baggy jeans. I remember turning up being like, “That’s not you.” Skating is a part of who I am, but I was looking to represent myself in some way, shape, or form.

Then we started this indie band when I was 16, 17. Devonté Hynes had this band called Test Icicles. I always used to look at those guys with their skinny jeans and their big hair, and I was just like, “That’s a bit of me, that.” How skinny can my jeans get? How drain pipe-y am I? That’s where I really started to find my own identity.

I’ve been fortunate enough throughout my career to meet and work with such beautiful creative people in fashion and find myself more within that, too. I was talking about it to somebody yesterday: When you try a fit on that is not you, it’s like having a bad haircut. You don’t want to do that. I’m even the same if I’m doing a photoshoot. I always go through the rail and I’ll say, “That’s not my vibe. I can’t say that I’m going to wear that.” Of course, I’m always willing to try, I’m always willing to push. But you know yourself better as you get older.

It was from Alexander McQueen. I loved the identity of that brand, but I couldn’t afford a jacket, or a suit, or even a scarf. But the smaller pieces, the rings and the wallets, were like 100 bucks. Those were the things that I would gravitate towards and buy.

More recently, within the last 10 years, I remember coming here to New York for a show that I did called Will, going to Bergdorf, and buying a couple of pairs of Comme des Garçons trousers. As they were being rung up, I was like, “All right.” It wasn’t loads—we’re not talking thousands—but it was still a lot of money. That was probably the first big clothing purchase that I ever made. And I’ve still got the trousers. I used to wear them on stage in the band as well, which is foolish.

Got a bunch of stuff from H. Lorenzo the other day—some great shirts, some great jackets. I really like how they curate the store. My most recent purchase is a lot of stuff from the new Ann Demeulemeester collection. I actually just bought a sick leather trench from it—brown leather, which is fire.

Jacket by Thom Browne. Shirt, jeans, shoes by Ann Demeulemeester.

Going back to when we were kids: Test Icicles, the Libertines, the Rakes, Franz Ferdinand, Editors. Got to meet a few of those guys throughout my travels, which was always pretty sick. Nick Cave. Warren Ellis. Nick has got such a sharp style, as does Warren. Warren’s a bit more unbuttoned. I met Warren in Venice five years ago. He was stood at the end of the pier and I was so excited to meet him, I just bounded up. I was like, “Hi, Mr. Ellis. My name’s Jamie.” And I just blurted out to him for ages, and then I was like, “Thank you so much.” He said, "Good to meet you, mate. Bye.”

I think fluidity and being myself is always the main thing. I’ve never felt wholly comfortable in a regular suit. I remember we were invited to do a show in Venice, and the band that we were in was pretty heavy. We wore suits in an environment that for us felt almost quite subversive. The music that we played didn’t really fit that. I quite enjoyed that.

But on the whole, I don’t love suits too much. I like to keep it more interesting and fluid. I’m not saying that they can’t be interesting for other people, but I’ve never been interested [in them myself]. Apart from McQueen, but that’s because something like the McQueen shoulder is so identifiable and creates such an incredible silhouette. That’s probably the only time I’ve ever really been like, “I can wear this suit for a long time.” But yeah, I avoid anything that doesn’t feel right for me.

It’s hard to say. I do feel like so often they can blend. I’ve been so fortunate in my career, being drawn to things that feel like me and getting to explore different parts of myself on film. That does have an effect on the music that I’m making at the time.

With a film or a television series, you’re saying someone else’s words and building a character, but also at times injecting your own personal experience into that. In music, they are your words. You can make a choice to be like, “I’m going to build a world in this song to express something.” Or I can just be like, “This is me.” So, they can scratch different itches, but I think that they work in symbiosis sometimes.

Whenever my scalp feels tight and itchy and I notice white flakes falling, I wonder whether my love of hot showers (yes, I’m guilty of turning my small NYC shower into the equivalent of a hot spring) or my daily use of hot styling tools might be contributing. Whatever the cause, I know it’s time to give my scalp some extra attention.

As Hadley King, MD, a New York City board-certified dermatologist, explains, dry skin is generally characterized by water loss and a disrupted skin barrier. The same applies to the scalp, which Dr. King says needs both water-binding ingredients and barrier-supporting lipids to stay moisturized.

Several things can cause a dry scalp. Morgan Rabach, MD, a board-certified dermatologist and cofounder of LM Medical NYC, lists overwashing, using hot water in the shower, excessive hot tool use, and overprocessing hair with harsh chemicals as habits that may contribute. Certain skin conditions, like eczema or seborrheic dermatitis, and environmental factors such as cold weather or low humidity are also common causes.

Additionally, Y. Claire Chang, MD, a board-certified dermatologist at UnionDerm, adds that sebum production can decrease with age and during hormonal changes, making your scalp even more prone to dryness. These are all things you’ll want to address because, as we know, healthy hair comes from a healthy scalp. “The scalp is an extension of the skin on the face and body,” says Dr. Chang. “It is important to maintain a healthy skin barrier on the scalp just like the rest of the body.”

Luckily, it’s not too hard to keep your scalp moisturized. Just consider adding the following steps to your routine.

The first step to moisturizing your scalp is washing it with a gentle shampoo formulated with hydrating ingredients like glycerin, ceramides, and hyaluronic acid. Dr. King agrees and recommends using a gentle, non-medicated shampoo rather than a harsher clarifying shampoo if the scalp is dry. “The goal is to remove sweat, sebum, and product buildup without stripping the scalp’s protective lipids,” she says.

She says to look for gentle surfactants and recommends a shampoo like the Nutrire S.1 Calm Shampoo for Dry Scalp, which contains humectants like glycerin and panthenol to retain water and watermelon seed oil to provide emollient lipids that smooth dry skin. Alexis Stephens, DO, a board-certified dermatologist based in Coral Springs, Florida, likes the Vanicream Shampoo for Sensitive Skin as it is made without several of the most common irritants found in products, such as fragrance and essential oils. “It’s a good option for people with sensitive scalps or those who experience irritation from fragranced hair products,” Dr. Stephens says. “While it isn’t a moisturizer itself, it helps establish a gentler cleansing routine that supports scalp comfort.”

Like your face, your scalp skin can get dry when you overdo exfoliation. “A dry scalp generally doesn’t need aggressive scrubbing,” Dr. King says. “If someone has significant scale, it’s important to determine whether we’re dealing with seborrheic dermatitis or psoriasis rather than simply trying to exfoliate it away.”

After shampooing, Dr. Chang recommends using a moisturizing scalp treatment. Look for nourishing ingredients like hyaluronic acid, glycerin, or panthenol for that added moisture. You’ll want to part your hair into sections to apply the product directly to the scalp, she says, and she recommends something like the Kérastase Nutritive Hydrating Scalp Serum; it’s a lightweight leave-in treatment made with plant-based proteins, glycerin, panthenol, and niacinamide to provide targeted hydration. Dr. King likes The Ordinary Natural Moisturizing Factors + HA for Scalp, which she says is packed with moisturizing factors that replicate components naturally found in skin to help keep the skin hydrated.

Conditioning your hair is still an important part of your routine, particularly if you’re experiencing dryness along the hair shaft as well as on your scalp. Dr. Stephens says this is especially important for curly and coily hair textures, which may need more conditioning along the hair shaft even when the scalp itself isn’t dry. She likes the CeraVe Gentle Hydrating Conditioner, which contains known hydrating ingredients such as hyaluronic acid, niacinamide, and glycerin to support the skin barrier. “It’s also suitable for all curl patterns, including curly and coily hair, and helps leave the hair feeling softer and more manageable after cleansing,” she says.

Dr. Chang recommends applying conditioner primarily to the midlengths and ends to keep hair hydrated and to reduce breakage. We like the Nécessaire The Conditioner, as it’s fragrance-free and made with nourishing ingredients like glycerin, ceramides, and hyaluronic acid to keep hair hydrated and healthy.

Environmental stressors like the sun’s harmful UV rays can exacerbate dryness, which is why Dr. Chang encourages patients to use proper sun protection, such as hats and scalp-friendly sunscreen (we like the Sun Bum SPF 30 Sunscreen Scalp and Hair Mist Spray or the Coola Scalp Hair Spray Sunscreen SPF 30 Mist) on exposed areas. This is particularly important for anyone with thinning hair or a visible scalp.

Though it can feel soothing, Dr. Chang says to avoid washing your hair in excessively hot water, as it can dry out your scalp. Instead, use lukewarm water and keep your showers short to avoid stripping your scalp of its natural oils.

You’ll also want to avoid excessive product buildup, as heavy oils, dry shampoos, and styling products can accumulate on the scalp and potentially contribute to irritation. Regular cleansing will be key, so use the right water temperature.

Anyone can experience a dry scalp, regardless of skin tone, skin type, or hair texture, Dr. Stephens says. But people with sensitive skin, eczema, or a history of contact dermatitis may be more susceptible. Dr. Chang adds that lifestyle and environmental factors (think cold weather, low humidity, and indoor heating during the winter), as well as age, can play a role.

What Is the Difference Between Dry Scalp and Dry Hair?

Distinguishing between dry scalp and dry hair matters when you’re trying to find the best products to address each concern. “One of the biggest misconceptions I see, particularly among patients with curly and coily hair, is that dry hair automatically means dry scalp,” Dr. Stephens says. “It doesn’t. Tightly coiled hair is more prone to dryness along the hair shaft, partly because natural scalp oils don’t distribute as easily down the curls. But the scalp underneath may be perfectly balanced or even oily. That’s why I encourage people to think of their scalp and hair as two areas with different needs.”

Dr. Chang says to think of it like this: Hair dryness is about how moisture and natural oils travel along the hair shaft, while scalp dryness is more closely related to skin barrier function, sebum production, underlying skin conditions, and environmental exposures.

What Ingredients Should You Avoid to Prevent a Dry Scalp?

Dr. Rabach lists hair dyes, fragrance, and certain alcohols as common culprits that can dry out the scalp and may be worth avoiding. Dr. Stephens agrees and adds that harsh cleansing formulas with alcohol can strip away too much of your scalp’s protective surface (especially when used too frequently) and can be drying or irritating.

Other ingredients to look out for, she says, are essential oils. “They don’t necessarily dry out the scalp directly, but they can trigger irritation or allergic contact dermatitis, which may leave the scalp feeling tight, itchy, or uncomfortable,” she says.

With ingredients like salicylic acid, which help with scalp issues such as dandruff, you still want to be careful, as they may worsen dryness if you use them too often. She adds that just because something is labeled “sulfate-free,” it doesn’t automatically mean it's gentle. You want to consider the formulation as a whole. “It’s important to remember that the overall formulation matters more than any single ingredient,” she says.

What Is the Difference Between Dry Scalp and Dandruff?

Dr. Chang says flaking doesn’t always mean your scalp is dry. Dandruff is generally considered a mild form of seborrheic dermatitis, a condition associated with Malassezia yeast, scalp oils, and inflammation. You’ll need a special type of treatment for these scalp conditions, and it’s best to consult your dermatologist for a proper diagnosis.

Dr. King adds that if you’re experiencing persistent itching, redness, thick scales, crusting, significant flaking, or any pain, it may be time to seek professional help. “I’d recommend evaluation rather than assuming it’s simple dryness,” she says.

When we test and review a product, we take a holistic approach to deliver well-rounded product recommendations. First, we lean on Vogue’s vast network of experts—from board-certified dermatologists to celebrity estheticians—to gain professional insight into the industry’s standout products, ones these specialists would actually use on their clients. We pair their expertise with our editorial best practices to curate the thoughtful edits you read on our site.

For scalp moisturizing products, we selected the best based on ingredients, texture, ease of application, finish, and the hair-care concerns they address. To do this, we paired our personal tests of each formula with expert guidance and reviewer insights to determine what we would recommend. Read more about our testing methodology here.

#6704. Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

#6703. Turkey Pot Pie

Chicken pot pie is a perfect cozy dinner for chilly fall days, but like most classics, it could use an upgrade. This turkey pot pie is a perfect way to switch up your meal rotation and make sure those Thanksgiving turkey leftovers don’t go to waste. That being said, this dinner is so comforting, it deserves to be made all season long.

What People Are Saying:“This was AMAZING. The filling is delicious, the crust is super flaky and golden brown. I will make this again for sure.” - GoldTeepee

Pop your butter in the freezer for about 15 minutes before you start making the crust so it’s adequately cold. Grab a large food processor and pulse together the flour, sugar, and salt until they’re mixed. Toss in the butter and pulse again until you see pea-sized pieces and larger chunks.

With the motor running, add vinegar and four tablespoons of ice water, one tablespoon at a time, until the dough just comes together and becomes moist. Make sure the dough isn’t wet and sticky or too crumbly (you can test this by squeezing some with your fingers). If the dough is too crumbly and not coming together, add more ice water, 1 teaspoon at a time.

Turn the dough out onto a lightly floured surface and gently squeeze it together. Knead it just a couple of times so it comes together, then split it into two balls. Flatten each one into a smooth disk, wrap them up in plastic, and pop them in the fridge for at least an hour or even overnight if you want to get ahead.

Move your oven rack to the center, then preheat to 375°. Grab a big, deep skillet and melt the butter over medium heat. Toss in the onions and carrots, and stir until they’re soft. Give it about 7 to 8 minutes. Next, add the garlic and cook, stirring, just until it smells amazing (about a minute). Now, grab a spatula or wooden spoon and stir in the flour. Cook, scraping up any tasty bits from the bottom, until the mixture turns golden and starts to bubble—just 2 or 3 minutes.

Pour the wine in slowly, stirring as you go. Let it simmer for about 3 minutes, just until that alcohol smell is gone. Then, slowly add 1 1/3 cups of cream, still scraping up all the good stuff from the bottom. Keep cooking until the mixture starts to boil and thickens up a bit. This should take around 5 minutes.

Fold in the turkey, peas, thyme, and parsley. Give it all a good season with kosher salt and pepper. Take the skillet off the heat and let the filling cool until you’re ready to use it.

Butter up a 9" pie dish or a deep skillet for your crust. On a lightly floured surface, roll out one disk of dough into a circle about 16" across and 1/4" thick. Carefully lay the dough into the pie dish, letting the edges slump down naturally. Trim the dough, leaving roughly a 1" overhang. Finally, pour in the cooled filling.

Roll out the second disk of dough into a 16"-diameter round about 1/4" thick and arrange it on top of the filling. Fold the top overhang into the bottom, pressing firmly to seal. Crimp the edges if you’d like. Using a paring knife, cut slits on top, and brush with the remaining 2 tablespoons of cream and sprinkle with sea salt.

Bake the pie (cover the edges with foil if they start getting too brown) until the crust is golden and the filling is bubbling. This takes about 1 hour 15 minutes. Once it’s done, move the pie to a wire rack and let it cool for about 15 minutes before digging in.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Cover your pot pie tightly with plastic wrap or store in an airtight container in the fridge for up to five days after baking. If you’d like to make your pot pie ahead of time and freeze it, wrap the whole (baked or unbaked) turkey pot pie tightly in plastic wrap and store in the freezer for up to 2 months.

#6702. From Rihanna to Rosalía, These Are Martine Rose’s Biggest Celebrity Superfans

At last, the news has officially broken: Martine Rose has been appointed to the helm of Balenciaga. While expectations of the announcement have been brewing for the past few months, it’s one that has been met with pretty much ubiquitous celebration.

That’s not to dismiss the achievements of her predecessor, Pierpaolo Piccioli, whose tenure was marked by a sculptural, romantic flair and a rich sense for color and textural play. Still, the warmth expressed for the British designer’s appointment is uniquely multifaceted. There’s its representational significance, as she joins a growing coterie of women of color at the helm of fashion’s most influential houses, but beyond that—and arguably more importantly—is her skill as a designer, and its capacity to shape the fashion conversation at large.

That’s something she’s more than proved at her namesake label, where her tweaked-and-twisted, often quietly kinky riffs on the everyday dress codes she observes in her native London have been key in bridging the gap between the realms of streetwear and high fashion over the past decade. There is also, as anyone versed in their menswear lore will know, the fact that Rose’s big break arguably came at Balenciaga, where she played an instrumental role in shaping the aesthetic of the house, working alongside Demna during the early, agenda-setting years of his tenure. And then, as we’ve come to know over the years, there’s Martine Rose herself: one of the sharpest and funniest voices the industry has in its midst.

You don’t have to look far for proof of just how widely her influence has spread. Though often framed as something of a fashion insider’s favorite, Rose has an equally devoted A-list following. Rihanna is regularly spotted in her designs, while Kendrick Lamar has all but appointed her his de facto dresser for some of the biggest moments of his career, wearing custom Rose looks to collect his Best Rap Album Grammy in 2023 and for his critically acclaimed 2025 Super Bowl half-time performance.

Below, revisit the moments your favorite celebrities repped one of fashion’s favorite designers.

In October 2025, Justin Bieber was spotted in LA wearing a graphic, color-blocked, logo-emblazoned sweater by Martine Rose.

Rihanna is a Martine Rose superfan. In May 2025, she was seen sporting one of the designer’s signature striped polos and baggy-fit jeans on the streets of New York, shortly after revealing her baby bump at that year’s Met Gala.

We’re naturally biased, but one of our favorite Martine Rose moments is without doubt when Billie Eilish graced the cover of our British Vogue’s May 2025 issue, sporting a hot-pink track jacket and headscarf in an updated riff on Balmoral chic.

At the 2025 Super Bowl, Kendrick Lamar—another of Martine Rose’s highest profile superfans—wore a full custom look by the designer for his critically-lauded half-time show, single-handedly reinvigorating the market for denim flares.

In 2025, Timothée Chalamet opted for Martine Rose tailoring for the London premiere of A Complete Unknown, shortly after being spotted in LA wearing one of the brand’s distressed caps.

Kendrick Lamar’s penchant for wearing the brand goes back further than his Super Bowl performance. In 2023, he wore a full look—including a customized track jacket and a then-unreleased colorway of the designer’s viral Nike Shox MR4 mules—to pick up the Grammy for that year’s best rap album.

For further proof of the Biebers’s appreciation for the sportier side of Martine Rose’s offering, look no further than a 2023 Hailey Bieber.

…and here in New York, just a month later.

Rosalía’s appetite for an IYKYK style staple is renowned—as proved by her status as an early adopter of the Nike Shox MR4 in 2022, one of the most hotly coveted products from Rose’s longstanding collaboration with the sports giant.

Proving a Martine Rose track jacket’s irrefutable grail status, Rihanna was repping hers as early as 2022.

#6701. 11 Best Cowboy Boots in 2026, According to GQ Editors

You might think that cowboy boots are a privilege reserved for ranch hands and folks who can actually ride a horse. But with a little chutzpah, the best cowboy boots are just as adept on a saddle as they are on the subway. Is that so surprising? Before they blossomed into their fashionable forms, much of menswear’s most riffed on garments were rooted in function: cargo pants, work jackets, even suits. With enough time, they were adopted by civilians and adapted to their second lives as symbols of self-expression and creativity, not just job uniforms. Cowboy boots are no different.

In terms of styling, the classic move for western boots is to lean into their rougher side. Toss them on with some well-fitting jeans (preferably vintage boot cuts) and with a snap shirt. And that's still a great approach. But if you open up your mind and step outside of the saloon, the possibilities are practically endless. A slick pair of exotic leather cowboy boots matched with a ‘70s-inspired suit screams filthy rich oil tycoon if not Alessandro Michele-era Gucci. Or, why not mix up a preppy pair of chinos with a grungy graphic tee and some roughed-up suede ropers? The point is, you don’t have to pretend to be a cowboy to wear their boots. So treat them like any other pair of shoes in your closet and wear them however you want. Hell, we’d go so far as to call them an essential pair of boots for every wardrobe.

And if you’re having trouble, well, that’s why you’re here. We’ve wrangled together the best cowboy boots west—and east—of the Mississippi, from the budget-friendly to the ostentatious and every vibe in-between.

The good folks at Tecovas are living, breathing proof that direct-to-consumer brands aren’t all operated by algorithms tasked with solving imaginary problems. The DTC upstart might be the youngest of the bootmakers on this list, but it's quickly endeared itself to budget-strapped swashbucklers with a hankering for democratically-priced kicks.

Take, for example, the Cartwright, a handsome riff on a classic western silhouette made in Leon, Mexico, a bona fide cobbling capital of the world with over a century of expertise to draw on. It boasts hand-laid cording at the shaft, a resoleable Goodyear-welt construction, and a slew of colors and leathers to choose from, including genuine cowhide and goat leather. They’re not the cheapest boots on this list, but the relatively approachable price belies the craftsmanship involved. For $375, they’re one small step up from our favorite budget cowboy boots—but one giant leap in overall quality.

You can think of roper boots as the chilled-out version of the average western boot. Originally designed for calf roping, roper boots feature a shorter shaft and a shorter, squared off heel. These details made it easier for cowboys to dismount their horse and run after the calves they roped. Coincidentally, they also make roper boots easier to walk in which is why some people prefer them over other cowboy boots for everyday wear.

Our pick for the best roper boots currently goes to Red Wing. (Perhaps no surprise, given the brand also makes our favorite trend-proof boots.) Part of Red Wing's Heritage line, they're crafted with premium S.B. Foot Tanning Company leather, and feature Goodyear welt construction so you can have them resoled and keep ‘em going for a long time. Plus, if you’re just dipping your toes into the cowboy boot world, the minimalist uppers forgo the decorative western stitching which makes them easier to style.

If you’re after that western look but need a pair of boots that can handle the demands of a jobsite, a lot of guys will tell you to look to Ariat. That’s because they manage to blend classic cowboy style with modern-day features, and a palatable price point in perfect proportion. While they do offer a range of work boots in lace-up styles, their Groundbreaker boots are a standout with classic cowboy boot looks.

They’re made of full-grain leather, include a supportive and comfortable insole, and meet ASTM standards for slip resistance and electrical safety. Because it’s among Ariat’s most popular styles, it’s also available in a wide range of colorways, toe shapes, and even steel toe versions. Some more traditional cowboys will poo-poo the fact that these aren’t made stateside, but if you’re on a budget, you’ll get more than what you pay for.

Cowboy boots aren’t all rough-and-tumble affairs. In fact, the right pair can easily strut the red carpet or waltz into a fancy restaurant with panache. You’ll want a pair with leather that shines up well and in a darker colorway. For date nights and more formal affairs, these Tony Lamas will impress thanks to the exotic lizard skin uppers and low-key embroidery. They’re the kind of boots that can play well for the in-laws with a tailored suit or play a rock-’n’-roll star with some vintage jeans and a tight white tee.

These days, most boot brands walk in the shadows of one brand: Lucchese. They’ve been outfitting American presidents, high-profile celebs, and the Dallas Cowboy Cheerleaders for decades and it’s all thanks to their commitment to high-quality craftsmanship. Though any pair of Lucchese’s would earn you more than a few approving head nods, the most coveted are the boots that they make in their Texas workshop.

Using a range of full-grain leathers and exotic leathers like caiman alligator and pirarucu fish skin, each pair is crafted by master bootmakers using time-honored techniques. The Gavin, in their iconic Black Cherry, is a picture-perfect style featuring smooth Santini goat leather uppers with intricate embellishments, welted construction, and lemonwood pegs—made the old-fashioned way, basically. They’ll cost you a pretty penny, of course, but they'll last pretty much forever, and the drip you’ll get in return is priceless.

From Ralph Lauren’s western-inspired sub-label, these RRL boots meld high-end materials with old-world craftsmanship and feature American-tanned leather uppers, Goodyear-welted construction, and vintage-style rubber soles—all crafted in a multi-generational Texas bootmaking factory.

Frye is another American brand with proven boot quality chops. (In fact, it claims to be America's oldest continually-operating boot company.) Its Roper boot has all the same strengths as Red Wing's, and comes in a non-roughout leather.

We don't typically include the same designers twice on one list, but Tecovas are that good. The Johnny is for anyone who wants a softer, slightly more charming boot than the eternal Cartwright up top.

For fellas whose style skews a little more regular-guy than rodeo, these lower-profile, lower-priced Ropers have a Goodyear welt and Vibram outsole. Bang for your, ahem, buck.

Wythe's playing-card-inspired boots feature all the bells and whistles, including premium leather inside and out, hand-applied details, lemonwood pegs, and second-to-none construction all-around. While some brands tap the expert bootmakers in Léon, Mexico to pump out high-quality mass-appeal boots, Wythe tapped these artisans to really let them cook.

All of Yuketen's shoes are perfect, which is a big part of the reason Drake's now carries them. And while they're best known for their moccasin styles, the brand makes an exceptionally handsome cowboy boot too. Really, they're just showing off now.

The classic move for western boots is to lean into their rougher side. Toss them on with well-fitting jeans (preferably vintage bootcuts) and a snap-button shirt. But open up your mind and step outside of the saloon and the possibilities are practically endless. A slick pair of exotic leather cowboy boots matched with a '70s-inspired suit screams filthy-rich oil tycoon—if not Alessandro Michele-era Gucci. Or why not mix up a preppy pair of chinos with a grungy graphic tee and some roughed-up suede ropers? The point is, you don’t have to pretend to be a cowboy to wear their boots (though you certainly can). So treat them like any other pair of shoes in your closet and wear them however you want. Hell, we’d go so far as to call them an essential pair of boots for every wardrobe.

Peter Middleton knows a thing or two about the lifestyle having cut his teeth at Ralph Lauren and used it as a springboard for his own western-inspired brand, Wythe. “To me the beauty and shape of the Cowboy Boot (and a lot of the original design intent) lies in its curves and that’s what makes a great boot SEXY. There isn't a lot of men's footwear that has these dramatic curves, leather, and a high heel but the right cowboy boot has them all.”

He says that good cowboy boots should be made with natural leathers that age well with wear, mould to the wearer’s feet, and can be recrafted repeatedly. His non-negotiables include full leather construction from the insole to the outsole, linings, uppers, and heels. Look for Goodyear welted construction which will allow you to have the boots resoled and extend their life. The toe bug (the fancy stitching at the toe), should sit right where your foot flexes to help cover up the crease that comes with each step. Preferably, this would be corded by hand, of course.

Price points will vary, and you can get some well-made boots for around $300. The really great stuff will often be twice that much. Middleton says, “the best thing to do is wait and save up until you can buy the version you actually want because its impossible to cut corners and still deliver the product you want.” So if you can be patient, save up. If you can’t, try buying secondhand. But if you simply can’t wait, you’ll do well enough with plenty of the mid-tier brands until you’re ready to upgrade.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. #6698. Cider-Braised Sausage and Lentils

I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

#6696. Oven-Roasted Turkey

The perfect Thanksgiving turkey is easier to make than you might think. Whether you're a first-timer planning a Friendsgiving dinner for your closest pals or the one whose house the whole family gathers at year after year, this recipe will help make your turkey the star of the dinner table. Let this be the year you ace Thanksgiving hosting and find your annual go-to guide for everything—roasting time, thawing, the secret to perfectly browned skin—on how to present the perfect roast bird.

Remove the giblets, trussing, and pop-up thermometers from the turkey. Pat the turkey completely dry inside and out with paper towels. If you plan to cut the wishbone out now, face the turkey neck opening toward you and locate the V-shaped wishbone in the neck cavity. With a sharp and flexible boning knife, using a short but firm swiping motion, gently cut the bone from the breast meat by making long incisions on both sides of the bone. Pry the bone loose with a paper towel or clean kitchen towel and discard. Using your fingers, separate the turkey breast from the skin.

In a spice grinder or mortar and pestle, grind all of the spices until they're finely ground and well combined. This will allow the spices to adhere to the surface of the turkey, especially the dried thyme.

Cover the entire turkey with the seasoning mix, turning the turkey over to season the back as well. Be sure to season under the breast skin and in the cavity. Transfer the turkey to a roasting rack. Refrigerate, uncovered, until cold, at least 12 hours and up to 2 days.

Arrange a rack in the lower third of the oven with no rack above it; preheat to 450°. Gently pat the turkey with paper towels to remove any excess moisture. Place the shallot, lemon, garlic, fresh thyme, and sage in the turkey cavity and neck opening. Be sure not to overfill the turkey. Err on the side of not stuffing everything in if it doesn’t fit. The turkey cavity needs airflow to cook evenly, and blocking that airflow will result in a longer cook time and a drier turkey. Drizzle the turkey with oil. Insert a leave-in probe thermometer (if using) into the turkey thigh or breast and transfer the roasting pan to the oven.

Roast the turkey for 30 minutes. Reduce the oven temperature to 350°. Continue to roast until the temperature in the thickest part of the breast registers 155° and the thigh registers 165°, about 1 hour and 30 minutes more, up to 2 hours more, rotating once during cooking to help the skin brown evenly. Let the turkey rest, uncovered, for 45 minutes before carving.

The full list of ingredients and directions can be found in the recipe below.

Store any leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 4 days. Leftovers can also be frozen. Chill any carved turkey in the refrigerator until cold, then transfer to a freezer-safe bag or container and label it with the contents and date. Store in the deepest part of the freezer for up to 6 months.

#6694. Simple-Is-Best Stuffing

More than a decade after Victoria Granof introduced this classic Thanksgiving stuffing recipe, it remains a staff and fan favorite. As former test kitchen director Carla Lalli Music puts it, it’s “everything you want about stuffing—straight down the middle.”

The recipe earns its name: buttery bread, sautéed onions and celery, and plenty of fresh herbs, with no unnecessary extras. Irregular, torn pieces of crusty bread create craggy edges that turn golden and crisp, while the broth-and-egg mixture renders the tender, custardy middle. Fresh parsley, sage, rosemary, and thyme (sing it with us) bring familiar holiday flavor, backed by a generous amount of butter.

Homemade turkey stock is welcome, but good low-sodium chicken broth from a carton works well. (Or use vegetable broth to make this stuffing vegetarian.) Get the first bake out of the way a day ahead, saving the browning for just before dinner.

Pair it with the rest of our classic Thanksgiving menu →

Choose a sturdy, crusty loaf, such as pane Pugliese, a French white boule, or a country-style sourdough. Skip soft sandwich bread, which can turn mushy once the broth goes in. Weigh out 1 lb. before drying it—the 10-cup measurement is approximate—and don’t skip drying the torn bread in a low oven, even if your loaf is already a day old.

Why bake the stuffing covered, then uncovered?

The covered bake cooks the stuffing through while retaining moisture; the uncovered bake gives you a crisp, golden top. The interior should be tender and cohesive, not dried out. Keep an eye on the stuffing during the second bake rather than assuming it needs the full time. The finished stuffing should be golden and crisp on top and reach 165°F in the center.

Yes. Bake it covered up to three days ahead, until the center reaches 165°F, then let cool briefly and refrigerate within 2 hours. Save the uncovered browning step for serving day. Return the stuffing to a 350°F oven, uncovered, until crisp on top and 165°F in the center, about 45–60 minutes. For longer-term prep, follow our guide to making and freezing stuffing ahead.

What’s the difference between stuffing and dressing?

Stuffing usually refers to a mixture cooked inside a turkey, while dressing is baked separately—but plenty of cooks use the names interchangeably. We prefer versions cooked outside the turkey for the crisp top and edges, but feel free to call it whichever name you grew up using.

Looking for a different take? Try our Sausage-and-Herb Stuffing, Cornbread Dressing With Sausage and Corn Nuts, or any of our other favorite homemade stuffing recipes.

Preheat oven to 250°. Grease a 13x9x2" baking dish with unsalted butter and set aside. Scatter 1 lb. good-quality day-old white bread, torn into 1" pieces (about 10 cups), in a single layer on a rimmed baking sheet. Bake, stirring occasionally, until dried out, about 1 hour. Let cool; transfer to a very large bowl.

Meanwhile, melt ¾ cup unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium-high heat; add 2½ cups chopped yellow onions and 1½ cups ¼" slices celery to melted butter. Stir often until just beginning to brown, about 10 minutes. Add to bowl with dried bread; stir in ½ cup chopped flat-leaf parsley, 2 Tbsp. chopped fresh sage, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh rosemary, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh thyme, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. freshly ground black pepper. Drizzle in 1¼ cups low-sodium chicken broth and toss gently. Let cool.

Preheat oven to 350°. Whisk 2 large eggs and remaining 1¼ cups low-sodium chicken broth in a small bowl. Add to bread mixture; fold gently until thoroughly combined. Transfer to prepared dish, cover with foil, and bake until an instant-read thermometer inserted into the center of dressing registers 160°, 35–40 minutes.

Uncover dressing; continue to bake until set and top is golden brown and crisp, 35–45 minutes longer.

Do ahead: Dressing can be baked (before browning) 1 day ahead; uncover and let cool, then cover and chill. Uncover and bake until top is golden brown and crisp, 45–60 minutes.

Leftover stuffing? Use it up in our Winter Panzanella With Stuffing Croutons →

Editor’s note: We first published this Thanksgiving stuffing recipe in our November 2012 issue as ‘Simple Is Best Dressing’; it has been updated for style. Head this way for more of our favorite Thanksgiving dinner side dishes→

#6693. Broiled Salmon Teriyaki

Sometimes all it takes to make dinner feel special is a big, bold piece of protein. Case in point: This salty-sweet salmon glazed in a glossy teriyaki-style sauce. Brushed in two rounds with the quick sauce made with nothing more than sugar, soy sauce, sesame oil, and vinegar, the salmon sizzles under the broiler, charring as it takes on a smoky flavor. This recipe calls for one large piece of salmon, but you can use smaller fillets or opt for a white fish such as cod or halibut. Just note that the cooking time will be shorter if using smaller pieces, so keep an eye on them. Add a quick garnish of sliced scallions and toasted sesame seeds, and dinner is done.

More salmon winners this way: Hot Honey-Glazed Salmon; Green Curry-Glazed Salmon; and Slow-Roasted Salmon With Harissa.

Bring ⅓ cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. unseasoned rice vinegar, and 2 tsp. toasted sesame oil to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat; cook until reduced by half and syrupy, 5–7 minutes. Let sauce cool until thickened slightly, about 10 minutes.

Heat broiler (if broiler is in your oven, place rack in upper third). Season both sides of one 1½–2-lb. skinless or skin-on center-cut salmon fillet with kosher salt. Place, skin side down, in a skillet or baking dish. Transfer one third of sauce to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Brush about half of remaining sauce over fillet. (If the salmon has a lot of room around it in the pan, line with foil to prevent runoff sauce from burning onto pan.)

Broil salmon until sauce is just starting to burn in spots, 4–7 minutes. Brush remaining sauce over fillet and broil until deeply charred and salmon is opaque all the way through, about 5 minutes.

Remove fish from oven and spoon reserved sauce over. Top with thinly sliced scallions and/or toasted sesame seeds if desired.

#6691. The 9 Most-Wanted Accessories of Fall—and How to Style Them Now

Among all the standout pieces on our fall shopping lists, it was the accessories that emerged as the real heroes. Both the fall and spring collections placed a renewed emphasis on personal style, with accessories offering some of the most compelling ways to make a look your own.

A necklace becomes more personal with the addition of collected charms, while a blazer or knit takes on new character with a brooch pinned to its lapel. Just as important is how these accessories are worn. Consider the strand of pearls layered beneath a sheer knit at The Row, or the silk scarf fastened around the waist like a cummerbund, rather than tied around the neck, at Polo Ralph Lauren. Sometimes, the smallest styling decisions make the biggest impact.

What these accessories have in common, beyond their styling potential, is their desirability. Between the fashion month street style set, our editors' own wish lists and wardrobes, and the collections we've seen since the fall shows, a clear picture has emerged of the accessories everyone wants to wear. Below, we've rounded up the season's most coveted pieces, along with a styling formula for each. From tasseled loafers to sculptural earrings, consider this your guide to the finishing touches that make an outfit.

Never underestimate the styling power of a delicate white floral brooch. Chanel's iconic camellia appeared in both the fall and spring collections, inspiring showgoers throughout fashion month to pin their own floral flourishes onto jackets and coats. The accessory has also become a favorite among Vogue editors (myself included), thanks to its ability to transform even the simplest outerwear. To offset its inherent femininity, try pairing one with a graphic T-shirt and a tailored blazer.

If there was one shoe silhouette that dominated the season, it was the pump. Lace-up iterations from Marni and Prada were particularly covetable, bringing a tougher, more directional attitude to an otherwise ladylike classic. Their appeal extends well beyond the traditionally feminine dresser. Lean into their unconventional proportions with a pair of skirted trousers and a brightly colored knit.

This is one trend I've had particular fun experimenting with, not least because it can be achieved with a simple rectangular silk scarf. Fold it in half lengthwise, wrap it around your waist, and knot it at the back, keeping the front wide and flat. It's a small styling trick that has transformed my trousers and tailoring, lending even a plain white T-shirt a certain polish. For the full effect, take a cue from Polo Ralph Lauren and embrace tuxedo-inspired dressing, right down to the patent leather slip-ons.

Eclectic charm necklaces were everywhere on the fall runways, from Celine and Altuzarra to Dries Van Noten and Marni. But what makes this jewelry trend especially appealing is the opportunity to make it entirely your own. You could, of course, invest in a ready-made version from Celine, but there's something even more charming about collecting medallions, keepsakes, and pendants over time and stringing them together yourself. Let a classic khaki trench and a fluted skirt provide the perfect backdrop.

Of all the re-edition Fendi Baguettes that caught our attention this season, the tiger-print version stood out for its nostalgic appeal. After several seasons of leopard print—and a sprinkling of zebra in the resort collections—tiger stripes offer a fresh alternative within the animal-print family. The trick is to let the print do the talking. Pair a tiger-striped bag with sleek black separates, such as a leather trench, knit dress, and ballet flats.

Call it the Phoebe Philo effect: The oversized statement earring is back, this time in sculptural clusters and explosive, burst-like shapes. What makes these earrings particularly interesting isn't just their scale, but the nonchalance with which they're worn. Rather than saving them for special occasions, consider them a form of everyday extravagance. A pair can do wonders for an otherwise understated combination of white jeans, a leather jacket, and ankle boots.

One reliable measure of an accessory's desirability? How difficult it is to get your hands on one. The Row's Calden tassel loafers have proved particularly elusive, cementing the menswear-inspired silhouette as one of fall's most-wanted shoes. Their appeal lies in their versatility: polished enough for tailoring, yet relaxed enough for everyday wear. A lived-in denim-on-denim look is just one way to put them to work.

At The Row, a simple strand of pearls was worn beneath a sheer, long-sleeved turtleneck rather than over it. The effect was subtle, unexpected, and remarkably chic. It's precisely this kind of styling that has brought the classic pearl necklace back into focus, though there's still plenty to be said for the traditional double-wrapped strand. Look to jewelry favorites Chan Luu and Sophie Buhai, as well as Toteme, for modern interpretations of the heirloom staple. Pearls also played a key styling role in By Malene Birger's lookbooks and on Valentino's runway, further proving their renewed appeal.

Belts have long been an essential finishing touch, but this season, it's the details that deserve a closer look. At Tory Burch's fall show, woven leather belts replaced their smooth counterparts—a seemingly minor distinction that made all the difference. Removed from their usual coastal-prep context, braided belts take on a decidedly more downtown attitude. Try one threaded through a pair of relaxed corduroys, finished with a purple barn jacket for an unexpected pop of color.
